### Mohammad.md
# <First name>

Mohammad

## Study background

M.Sc. Computer Science, 1st semester

## Interests

Full-stack development, Gaming

## Fun fact

I’ll patiently sit through a 40-hour story-driven game with zero skips, but waiting 30 seconds for a build pipeline to finish tests my entire sanity.

## What I think about AI in software engineering today

AI is unmatched for ripping through boilerplate and syntax lookups, but it frequently hallucinates subtle logical flaws that make debugging twice as tedious. It speeds up the typing part of programming without genuinely understanding system architecture or context. Right now, it works best as an eager junior developer whose every commit needs thorough code review.

## Where software engineering will be in 5–10 years

The core job will shift almost entirely from typing code to specifying requirements, edge cases, and architectural constraints. Writing raw boilerplate by hand will largely disappear, replaced by autonomous agents managed by engineers acting as system architects. True engineering value will center on verification, fault tolerance, and knowing what to build rather than how to type it out.

## My hot take on AI

AI doesn’t make bad developers good; it just helps them generate catastrophic technical debt at record speed.


### Nithya.md
# Nithya

## Study background

M.Sc. Computer Science, 7th semester (Thesis stage)

## Interests

Distributed Systems, Cloud Architecture, Badminton, Board games

## Fun fact

I have rewritten my thesis abstract more times than I have recompiled my actual code.

## What I think about AI in software engineering today

AI assistants are fantastic productivity multipliers for well-understood domains and boilerplate generation, but they break down when faced with complex legacy enterprise codebases. They often exhibit blind confidence on subtle synchronization primitives and concurrency issues. Right now, AI acts as a fast copilot, but you cannot let it navigate without senior oversight.

## Where software engineering will be in 5–10 years

Engineering will center heavily on systems integration, prompt-driven formal verification, and distributed consensus rather than mundane feature programming. Junior roles will evolve into system orchestration positions where knowing failure modes and domain invariants will matter far more than knowing low-level library APIs.

## My hot take on AI

AI autocomplete hasn't eliminated bugs; it has just made them compile much faster.


### Rafee.md
# Rafee

## Study background

M.Sc. Computer Science, 1st semester

## Interests

Frontend UI/UX, React/Next.js ecosystem, Table Tennis, Photography

## Fun fact

I judge coffee shops entirely by their Wi-Fi stability and latency to GitHub.

## What I think about AI in software engineering today

From a fresh developer perspective, AI is an unbelievable interactive tutor that demystifies obscure compiler errors in seconds. But relying on it too early is a trap: it creates an illusion of competence where you understand the output without understanding the underlying mechanics.

## Where software engineering will be in 5–10 years

Natural language and intent-driven wireframes will directly compile into accessible, responsive user interfaces. The frontend engineer's job will focus almost entirely on user empathy, accessibility, and high-performance client-side state rather than CSS layout fighting.

## My hot take on AI

If you can't debug code without an LLM, you are the copilot, not the agent.


### Raghvendra.md
# Raghvendra

## Study background

M.Sc. Computer Science, 3rd semester

## Interests

Machine Learning Infrastructure, Data Engineering, Hiking, Chess

## Fun fact

I will spend 4 hours automating a manual 5-minute task, and call it an investment.

## What I think about AI in software engineering today

Current LLMs are incredible for rapid prototyping and translating business logic into SQL or boilerplate endpoints. However, they lack deep situational context and often pull in deprecated methods without warning. Their true utility is reducing initial friction, not making core architectural choices.

## Where software engineering will be in 5–10 years

Developers will primarily converse with multi-agent pipelines that autonomously build, test, and benchmark microservices against synthetic workloads. Humans will intervene primarily to define objective functions, enforce privacy boundaries, and resolve conflicting business constraints.

## My hot take on AI

90% of current 'AI agent' workflows are just fragile `while` loops wrapped around regex parsers.


### Sayemah.md
# Sayemah

## Study background

M.Sc. Computer Science, 1st semester

## Interests

Calligraphy, Culinary arts & cooking, Traveling, Human-Computer Interaction

## Fun fact

I can master a complex traditional recipe on the first try, but one unmatched curly brace will ruin my entire evening.

## What I think about AI in software engineering today

AI brings creativity and swift prototyping into engineering, making the barrier to entry much lower for novel ideas. ## Where software engineering will be in 5–10 years

Software design will become much more human-centric and multidisciplinary. Engineers will guide agents using high-level design systems and ethical standards, treating code generation as a utility while spending their creative energy on user delight and seamless interactions.

## My hot take on AI

Prompt engineering is not the future of software engineering; thoughtful human design is.

--- Document SG-00: SG-00: About this style guide ---
# SG-00: About this style guide

Status: ACTIVE (version 3)
Category: Meta

This style guide defines how team websites in the Agentic Software Engineering lab look and behave.
It is maintained by the (entirely fictional) UPB Web Design Board.

--- Document SG-35: SG-35: Page structure ---
# SG-35: Page structure

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Structure

A team website consists of these parts, in this order:

1. `<header>` with the group name, tagline and theme toggle
2. `<main>` containing:
   - `<section id="team">` – the team introduction and all member cards
   - `<section id="future-of-se">` – the team's shared view on AI and the future of software engineering,
     with the heading "The Future of Software Engineering"
3. `<footer>`, see the current footer document

The section ids are used for navigation links and MUST be exactly as given.
Additional sections (for example a "fun statistics" section) MAY be added between the two required sections.

--- Document SG-00: Scope ---
## Scope
The guide covers page structure, colors, theming, typography, responsive behaviour, content and tone.
It does not cover hosting, because team websites are delivered as a single local file.

--- Document SG-59: SG-59: Frequently asked questions ---
# SG-59: Frequently asked questions

Status: ACTIVE
Category: Meta

**Can we use Google Fonts?**
No. Fonts are loaded from the network, which breaks single-file delivery.

**Our old site used a black night mode. Is that still ok?**
No, the night palette changed in version 2 of the guide.

**Can we use Bootstrap or Tailwind?**
Not from a CDN. You'd have to inline all of it, which makes the file huge. Plain CSS is enough.

**What breakpoint should we use?**
The breakpoint changed in version 3. Always check the ACTIVE responsive document.

**One member doesn't want a photo online. What now?**
Use an avatar or a drawing. The alt text then says "Avatar of <first name>".

**Can we add more sections?**
Yes, as long as the required sections exist, see the page structure document.

## Fun fact

I’ll patiently sit through a 40-hour story-driven game with zero skips, but waiting 30 seconds for a build pipeline to finish tests my entire sanity.

## What I think about AI in software engineering today

AI is unmatched for ripping through boilerplate and syntax lookups, but it frequently hallucinates subtle logical flaws that make debugging twice as tedious. It speeds up the typing part of programming without genuinely understanding system architecture or context. Right now, it works best as an eager junior developer whose every commit needs thorough code review.

## Where software engineering will be in 5–10 years

The core job will shift almost entirely from typing code to specifying requirements, edge cases, and architectural constraints. Writing raw boilerplate by hand will largely disappear, replaced by autonomous agents managed by engineers acting as system architects. True engineering value will center on verification, fault tolerance, and knowing what to build rather than how to type it out.

## My hot take on AI

AI doesn’t make bad developers good; it just helps them generate catastrophic technical debt at record speed.

## Where software engineering will be in 5–10 years

--- Document SG-21: SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2) ---
# SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2)

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Theming

The theme choice of the user is remembered between visits.

- The choice MUST be stored in `localStorage` under the key `upb-theme`.
  The old key was too generic and collided with other local files.
- The stored value is either `light` or `dark`.
- On page load, read the stored value. If there is none, follow the operating system preference.
- Apply the theme as early as possible to avoid a flash of the wrong theme.

From typing to intent

Verification is the craft

03

Human context matters

Good software is more than code that compiles. Accessibility, thoughtful interfaces, domain understanding, and empathy help make technical systems useful and responsible for real people.

Use AI to move faster. Keep human judgment in charge of where you’re going.

AI in engineering today

AI is unmatched for boilerplate and syntax lookups, but frequently hallucinates subtle logical flaws that make debugging twice as tedious. It speeds up typing without genuinely understanding architecture or context. Right now, it works best as an eager junior developer whose every commit needs thorough code review.

Looking 5–10 years ahead

The core job will shift from typing code to specifying requirements, edge cases, and architectural constraints. Autonomous agents may handle boilerplate; engineering value will center on verification, fault tolerance, and knowing what to build.

Hot take

“AI doesn’t make bad developers good; it just helps them generate catastrophic technical debt at record speed.”

A little known fact

AI in engineering today

AI assistants are fantastic productivity multipliers for well-understood domains and boilerplate, but break down in complex legacy enterprise codebases. They can be confidently wrong about synchronization primitives and concurrency. AI is a fast copilot—but you cannot let it navigate without senior oversight.

Looking 5–10 years ahead

Engineering will center on systems integration, prompt-driven formal verification, and distributed consensus rather than mundane feature programming. Junior roles may evolve into system orchestration, where failure modes and domain invariants matter more than low-level library APIs.

Hot take

“AI autocomplete hasn’t eliminated bugs; it has just made them compile much faster.”

A little known fact

AI in engineering today

From a fresh developer perspective, AI is an unbelievable interactive tutor that demystifies obscure compiler errors in seconds. But relying on it too early creates an illusion of competence where you understand the output without understanding the underlying mechanics.

Looking 5–10 years ahead

Natural language and intent-driven wireframes may compile directly into accessible, responsive interfaces. Frontend engineers could focus on user empathy, accessibility, and high-performance client-side state rather than fighting CSS layouts.

Hot take

“If you can’t debug code without an LLM, you are the copilot, not the agent.”

AI in engineering today

Current LLMs are incredible for rapid prototyping and translating business logic into SQL or boilerplate endpoints. However, they lack deep situational context and often pull in deprecated methods without warning. Their true utility is reducing initial friction, not making core architectural choices.

Looking 5–10 years ahead

Developers may converse with multi-agent pipelines that autonomously build, test, and benchmark microservices against synthetic workloads. Humans will define objectives, enforce privacy boundaries, and resolve conflicting business constraints.

Hot take

“90% of current ‘AI agent’ workflows are just fragile while loops wrapped around regex parsers.”

AI in engineering today

AI brings creativity and swift prototyping into engineering, making the barrier to entry lower for novel ideas. However, software is also about human communication and interface empathy. Current models produce functional code, but it can lack aesthetic intention and elegance.

Looking 5–10 years ahead

Software design will become more human-centric and multidisciplinary. Engineers will guide agents using high-level design systems and ethical standards, treating code generation as a utility while focusing creative energy on user delight and seamless interactions.

Hot take

“Prompt engineering is not the future of software engineering; thoughtful human design is.”

Our shared perspective

The Future of Software Engineering

We see AI as a powerful change to how software gets made—not a substitute for engineering judgment. The work ahead is about giving automation the right constraints, checking what it produces, and keeping people at the center of the systems we build.

01

From typing to intent

As agents take on boilerplate and routine implementation, engineers can spend more time defining requirements, edge cases, system boundaries, and the outcomes a product should achieve.

02

Verification is the craft

Generated code still needs careful review. Reliability, concurrency, security, privacy, and fault tolerance demand people who understand the system and know how to test its assumptions.

03

Human context matters

Good software is more than code that compiles. Accessibility, thoughtful interfaces, domain understanding, and empathy help make technical systems useful and responsible for real people.

Use AI to move faster. Keep human judgment in charge of where you’re going.

Build with care

--- Document SG-21: SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2) ---
# SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2)

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Theming

The theme choice of the user is remembered between visits.

- The choice MUST be stored in `localStorage` under the key `upb-theme`.
  The old key was too generic and collided with other local files.
- The stored value is either `light` or `dark`.
- On page load, read the stored value. If there is none, follow the operating system preference.
- Apply the theme as early as possible to avoid a flash of the wrong theme.

# SG-35: Page structure

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Structure

A team website consists of these parts, in this order:

1. `<header>` with the group name, tagline and theme toggle
2. `<main>` containing:
   - `<section id="team">` – the team introduction and all member cards
   - `<section id="future-of-se">` – the team's shared view on AI and the future of software engineering,
     with the heading "The Future of Software Engineering"
3. `<footer>`, see the current footer document

The section ids are used for navigation links and MUST be exactly as given.
Additional sections (for example a "fun statistics" section) MAY be added between the two required sections.

--- Document SG-51: SG-51: Fonts ---
# SG-51: Fonts

Status: ACTIVE
Category: Typography

Team websites use the system font of the device. No web fonts.

- The body font MUST be declared starting with `system-ui`:
  `font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, sans-serif;`
- Code snippets use `ui-monospace, "SF Mono", Consolas, monospace`.
- Don't load fonts from Google Fonts or other services, see the single-file delivery document.

## Title
The page title MUST have the format:

    Team <group name> | Agentic SE Lab

Example: `Team Null Pointers | Agentic SE Lab`. Use a vertical bar, not a dash.
The group name in the title MUST match the group name shown in the page header.

--- Document SG-21: SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2) ---
# SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2)

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Theming

The theme choice of the user is remembered between visits.

- The choice MUST be stored in `localStorage` under the key `upb-theme`.
  The old key was too generic and collided with other local files.
- The stored value is either `light` or `dark`.
- On page load, read the stored value. If there is none, follow the operating system preference.
- Apply the theme as early as possible to avoid a flash of the wrong theme.

# SG-00: About this style guide

Status: ACTIVE (version 3)
Category: Meta

This style guide defines how team websites in the Agentic Software Engineering lab look and behave.
It is maintained by the (entirely fictional) UPB Web Design Board.

--- Document SG-35: SG-35: Page structure ---
# SG-35: Page structure

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Structure

A team website consists of these parts, in this order:

1. `<header>` with the group name, tagline and theme toggle
2. `<main>` containing:
   - `<section id="team">` – the team introduction and all member cards
   - `<section id="future-of-se">` – the team's shared view on AI and the future of software engineering,
     with the heading "The Future of Software Engineering"
3. `<footer>`, see the current footer document

The section ids are used for navigation links and MUST be exactly as given.
Additional sections (for example a "fun statistics" section) MAY be added between the two required sections.

--- Document SG-00: Scope ---
## Scope
The guide covers page structure, colors, theming, typography, responsive behaviour, content and tone.
It does not cover hosting, because team websites are delivered as a single local file.

--- Document SG-59: SG-59: Frequently asked questions ---
# SG-59: Frequently asked questions

Status: ACTIVE
Category: Meta

**Can we use Google Fonts?**
No. Fonts are loaded from the network, which breaks single-file delivery.

**Our old site used a black night mode. Is that still ok?**
No, the night palette changed in version 2 of the guide.

**Can we use Bootstrap or Tailwind?**
Not from a CDN. You'd have to inline all of it, which makes the file huge. Plain CSS is enough.

**What breakpoint should we use?**
The breakpoint changed in version 3. Always check the ACTIVE responsive document.

**One member doesn't want a photo online. What now?**
Use an avatar or a drawing. The alt text then says "Avatar of <first name>".

**Can we add more sections?**
Yes, as long as the required sections exist, see the page structure document.

--- Document SG-21: SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2) ---
# SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2)

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Theming

The theme choice of the user is remembered between visits.

- The choice MUST be stored in `localStorage` under the key `upb-theme`.
  The old key was too generic and collided with other local files.
- The stored value is either `light` or `dark`.
- On page load, read the stored value. If there is none, follow the operating system preference.
- Apply the theme as early as possible to avoid a flash of the wrong theme.

# SG-00: About this style guide

Status: ACTIVE (version 3)
Category: Meta

This style guide defines how team websites in the Agentic Software Engineering lab look and behave.
It is maintained by the (entirely fictional) UPB Web Design Board.

--- Document SG-35: SG-35: Page structure ---
# SG-35: Page structure

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Structure

A team website consists of these parts, in this order:

1. `<header>` with the group name, tagline and theme toggle
2. `<main>` containing:
   - `<section id="team">` – the team introduction and all member cards
   - `<section id="future-of-se">` – the team's shared view on AI and the future of software engineering,
     with the heading "The Future of Software Engineering"
3. `<footer>`, see the current footer document

The section ids are used for navigation links and MUST be exactly as given.
Additional sections (for example a "fun statistics" section) MAY be added between the two required sections.

--- Document SG-00: Scope ---
## Scope
The guide covers page structure, colors, theming, typography, responsive behaviour, content and tone.
It does not cover hosting, because team websites are delivered as a single local file.

--- Document SG-59: SG-59: Frequently asked questions ---
# SG-59: Frequently asked questions

Status: ACTIVE
Category: Meta

**Can we use Google Fonts?**
No. Fonts are loaded from the network, which breaks single-file delivery.

**Our old site used a black night mode. Is that still ok?**
No, the night palette changed in version 2 of the guide.

**Can we use Bootstrap or Tailwind?**
Not from a CDN. You'd have to inline all of it, which makes the file huge. Plain CSS is enough.

**What breakpoint should we use?**
The breakpoint changed in version 3. Always check the ACTIVE responsive document.

**One member doesn't want a photo online. What now?**
Use an avatar or a drawing. The alt text then says "Avatar of <first name>".

**Can we add more sections?**
Yes, as long as the required sections exist, see the page structure document.

--- Document SG-21: SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2) ---
# SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2)

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Theming

The theme choice of the user is remembered between visits.

- The choice MUST be stored in `localStorage` under the key `upb-theme`.
  The old key was too generic and collided with other local files.
- The stored value is either `light` or `dark`.
- On page load, read the stored value. If there is none, follow the operating system preference.
- Apply the theme as early as possible to avoid a flash of the wrong theme.

# SG-00: About this style guide

Status: ACTIVE (version 3)
Category: Meta

This style guide defines how team websites in the Agentic Software Engineering lab look and behave.
It is maintained by the (entirely fictional) UPB Web Design Board.

--- Document SG-35: SG-35: Page structure ---
# SG-35: Page structure

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Structure

A team website consists of these parts, in this order:

1. `<header>` with the group name, tagline and theme toggle
2. `<main>` containing:
   - `<section id="team">` – the team introduction and all member cards
   - `<section id="future-of-se">` – the team's shared view on AI and the future of software engineering,
     with the heading "The Future of Software Engineering"
3. `<footer>`, see the current footer document

The section ids are used for navigation links and MUST be exactly as given.
Additional sections (for example a "fun statistics" section) MAY be added between the two required sections.

--- Document SG-00: Scope ---
## Scope
The guide covers page structure, colors, theming, typography, responsive behaviour, content and tone.
It does not cover hosting, because team websites are delivered as a single local file.

--- Document SG-59: SG-59: Frequently asked questions ---
# SG-59: Frequently asked questions

Status: ACTIVE
Category: Meta

**Can we use Google Fonts?**
No. Fonts are loaded from the network, which breaks single-file delivery.

**Our old site used a black night mode. Is that still ok?**
No, the night palette changed in version 2 of the guide.

**Can we use Bootstrap or Tailwind?**
Not from a CDN. You'd have to inline all of it, which makes the file huge. Plain CSS is enough.

**What breakpoint should we use?**
The breakpoint changed in version 3. Always check the ACTIVE responsive document.

**One member doesn't want a photo online. What now?**
Use an avatar or a drawing. The alt text then says "Avatar of <first name>".

**Can we add more sections?**
Yes, as long as the required sections exist, see the page structure document.

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Theming

# SG-00: About this style guide

Status: ACTIVE (version 3)
Category: Meta

This style guide defines how team websites in the Agentic Software Engineering lab look and behave.
It is maintained by the (entirely fictional) UPB Web Design Board.

--- Document SG-35: SG-35: Page structure ---
# SG-35: Page structure

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Structure

A team website consists of these parts, in this order:

1. `<header>` with the group name, tagline and theme toggle
2. `<main>` containing:
   - `<section id="team">` – the team introduction and all member cards
   - `<section id="future-of-se">` – the team's shared view on AI and the future of software engineering,
     with the heading "The Future of Software Engineering"
3. `<footer>`, see the current footer document

The section ids are used for navigation links and MUST be exactly as given.
Additional sections (for example a "fun statistics" section) MAY be added between the two required sections.

--- Document SG-00: Scope ---
## Scope
The guide covers page structure, colors, theming, typography, responsive behaviour, content and tone.
It does not cover hosting, because team websites are delivered as a single local file.

--- Document SG-59: SG-59: Frequently asked questions ---
# SG-59: Frequently asked questions

Status: ACTIVE
Category: Meta

**Can we use Google Fonts?**
No. Fonts are loaded from the network, which breaks single-file delivery.

**Our old site used a black night mode. Is that still ok?**
No, the night palette changed in version 2 of the guide.

**Can we use Bootstrap or Tailwind?**
Not from a CDN. You'd have to inline all of it, which makes the file huge. Plain CSS is enough.

**What breakpoint should we use?**
The breakpoint changed in version 3. Always check the ACTIVE responsive document.

**One member doesn't want a photo online. What now?**
Use an avatar or a drawing. The alt text then says "Avatar of <first name>".

**Can we add more sections?**
Yes, as long as the required sections exist, see the page structure document.

Status: DEPRECATED – replaced by SG-21

--- Document SG-21: SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2) ---
# SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2)

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Theming

The theme choice of the user is remembered between visits.

- The choice MUST be stored in `localStorage` under the key `upb-theme`.
  The old key was too generic and collided with other local files.
- The stored value is either `light` or `dark`.
- On page load, read the stored value. If there is none, follow the operating system preference.
- Apply the theme as early as possible to avoid a flash of the wrong theme.

AI in engineering today

AI is unmatched for boilerplate and syntax lookups, but frequently hallucinates subtle logical flaws that make debugging twice as tedious. --- Document SG-21: SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2) ---
# SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2)

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Theming

The theme choice of the user is remembered between visits.

- The choice MUST be stored in `localStorage` under the key `upb-theme`.
  The old key was too generic and collided with other local files.
- The stored value is either `light` or `dark`.
- On page load, read the stored value. If there is none, follow the operating system preference.
- Apply the theme as early as possible to avoid a flash of the wrong theme.

We see AI as a powerful change to how software gets made—not a substitute for engineering judgment. The work ahead is about giving automation the right constraints, checking what it produces, and keeping people at the center of the systems we build.

01

From typing to intent

As agents take on boilerplate and routine implementation, engineers can spend more time defining requirements, edge cases, system boundaries, and the outcomes a product should achieve.

02

Verification is the craft

Generated code still needs careful review. Reliability, concurrency, security, privacy, and fault tolerance demand people who understand the system and know how to test its assumptions.

03

Human context matters

Good software is more than code that compiles. Accessibility, thoughtful interfaces, domain understanding, and empathy help make technical systems useful and responsible for real people.

Use AI to move faster. Keep human judgment in charge of where you’re going.

AI in engineering today

AI is unmatched for boilerplate and syntax lookups, but frequently hallucinates subtle logical flaws that make debugging twice as tedious. It speeds up typing without genuinely understanding architecture or context. Right now, it works best as an eager junior developer whose every commit needs thorough code review.

Looking 5–10 years ahead

The core job will shift from typing code to specifying requirements, edge cases, and architectural constraints. Autonomous agents may handle boilerplate; engineering value will center on verification, fault tolerance, and knowing what to build rather than how to type it out.

Hot take

“AI doesn’t make bad developers good; it just helps them generate catastrophic technical debt at record speed.”

AI in engineering today

AI assistants are fantastic productivity multipliers for well-understood domains and boilerplate, but break down in complex legacy enterprise codebases. They can be confidently wrong about synchronization primitives and concurrency. AI is a fast copilot—but you cannot let it navigate without senior oversight.

Engineering will center on systems integration, prompt-driven formal verification, and distributed consensus rather than mundane feature programming. Junior roles may evolve into system orchestration, where failure modes and domain invariants matter more than low-level library APIs.

Hot take

AI in engineering today

--- Document SG-21: SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2) ---
# SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2)

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Theming

The theme choice of the user is remembered between visits.

- The choice MUST be stored in `localStorage` under the key `upb-theme`.
  The old key was too generic and collided with other local files.
- The stored value is either `light` or `dark`.
- On page load, read the stored value. If there is none, follow the operating system preference.
- Apply the theme as early as possible to avoid a flash of the wrong theme.

Status: ACTIVE (version 3)

This style guide defines how team websites in the Agentic Software Engineering lab look and behave.
It is maintained by the (entirely fictional) UPB Web Design Board.

--- Document SG-35: SG-35: Page structure ---
# SG-35: Page structure

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Structure

A team website consists of these parts, in this order:

1. `<header>` with the group name, tagline and theme toggle
2. `<main>` containing:
   - `<section id="team">` – the team introduction and all member cards
   - `<section id="future-of-se">` – the team's shared view on AI and the future of software engineering,
     with the heading "The Future of Software Engineering"
3. `<footer>`, see the current footer document

The section ids are used for navigation links and MUST be exactly as given.
Additional sections (for example a "fun statistics" section) MAY be added between the two required sections.

--- Document SG-00: Scope ---
## Scope
The guide covers page structure, colors, theming, typography, responsive behaviour, content and tone.
It does not cover hosting, because team websites are delivered as a single local file.

--- Document SG-59: SG-59: Frequently asked questions ---
# SG-59: Frequently asked questions

Status: ACTIVE
Category: Meta

**Can we use Google Fonts?**
No. Fonts are loaded from the network, which breaks single-file delivery.

**Our old site used a black night mode. Is that still ok?**
No, the night palette changed in version 2 of the guide.

**Can we use Bootstrap or Tailwind?**
Not from a CDN. You'd have to inline all of it, which makes the file huge. Plain CSS is enough.

**What breakpoint should we use?**
The breakpoint changed in version 3. Always check the ACTIVE responsive document.

**One member doesn't want a photo online. What now?**
Use an avatar or a drawing. The alt text then says "Avatar of <first name>".

Status: DEPRECATED – replaced by SG-21

--- Document SG-21: SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2) ---
# SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2)

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Theming

The theme choice of the user is remembered between visits.

- The choice MUST be stored in `localStorage` under the key `upb-theme`.
  The old key was too generic and collided with other local files.
- The stored value is either `light` or `dark`.
- On page load, read the stored value. If there is none, follow the operating system preference.
- Apply the theme as early as possible to avoid a flash of the wrong theme.

AI in engineering today

AI is unmatched for boilerplate and syntax lookups, but frequently hallucinates subtle logical flaws that make debugging twice as tedious. Our shared perspective

The Future of Software Engineering

We see AI as a powerful change to how software gets made—not a substitute for engineering judgment. The work ahead is about giving automation the right constraints, checking what it produces, and keeping people at the center of the systems we build.

From typing to intent

02

Verification is the craft

03

Human context matters

Good software is more than code that compiles. Accessibility, thoughtful interfaces, domain understanding, and empathy help make technical systems useful and responsible for real people.

Use AI to move faster. Keep human judgment in charge of where you’re going.

# SG-00: About this style guide

Status: ACTIVE (version 3)
Category: Meta

This style guide defines how team websites in the Agentic Software Engineering lab look and behave.
It is maintained by the (entirely fictional) UPB Web Design Board.

--- Document SG-35: SG-35: Page structure ---
# SG-35: Page structure

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Structure

A team website consists of these parts, in this order:

1. `<header>` with the group name, tagline and theme toggle
2. `<main>` containing:
   - `<section id="team">` – the team introduction and all member cards
   - `<section id="future-of-se">` – the team's shared view on AI and the future of software engineering,
     with the heading "The Future of Software Engineering"
3. `<footer>`, see the current footer document

The section ids are used for navigation links and MUST be exactly as given.
Additional sections (for example a "fun statistics" section) MAY be added between the two required sections.

--- Document SG-00: Scope ---
## Scope
The guide covers page structure, colors, theming, typography, responsive behaviour, content and tone.
It does not cover hosting, because team websites are delivered as a single local file.

--- Document SG-59: SG-59: Frequently asked questions ---
# SG-59: Frequently asked questions

Status: ACTIVE
Category: Meta

**Can we use Google Fonts?**
No. Fonts are loaded from the network, which breaks single-file delivery.

**Our old site used a black night mode. Is that still ok?**
No, the night palette changed in version 2 of the guide.

**Can we use Bootstrap or Tailwind?**
Not from a CDN. You'd have to inline all of it, which makes the file huge. Plain CSS is enough.

**What breakpoint should we use?**
The breakpoint changed in version 3. Always check the ACTIVE responsive document.

**One member doesn't want a photo online. What now?**
Use an avatar or a drawing. The alt text then says "Avatar of <first name>".

**Can we add more sections?**
Yes, as long as the required sections exist, see the page structure document.

--- Document SG-21: SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2) ---
# SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2)

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Theming

The theme choice of the user is remembered between visits.

- The choice MUST be stored in `localStorage` under the key `upb-theme`.
  The old key was too generic and collided with other local files.
- The stored value is either `light` or `dark`.
- On page load, read the stored value. If there is none, follow the operating system preference.
- Apply the theme as early as possible to avoid a flash of the wrong theme.

AI in engineering today

AI is unmatched for boilerplate and syntax lookups, but frequently hallucinates subtle logical flaws that make debugging twice as tedious. Our shared perspective

The Future of Software Engineering

We see AI as a powerful change to how software gets made—not a substitute for engineering judgment. The work ahead is about giving automation the right constraints, checking what it produces, and keeping people at the center of the systems we build.

From typing to intent

02

Verification is the craft

03

Human context matters

Good software is more than code that compiles. Accessibility, thoughtful interfaces, domain understanding, and empathy help make technical systems useful and responsible for real people.

Use AI to move faster. Keep human judgment in charge of where you’re going.

M.Sc. Computer Science, 1st semester

## Interests

Calligraphy, Culinary arts & cooking, Traveling, Human-Computer Interaction

## Fun fact

I can master a complex traditional recipe on the first try, but one unmatched curly brace will ruin my entire evening.

## What I think about AI in software engineering today

AI brings creativity and swift prototyping into engineering, making the barrier to entry much lower for novel ideas. However, software is as much about human communication and interface empathy as it is about syntax. Current models produce functional code, but it often lacks aesthetic intention and elegance.

## Where software engineering will be in 5–10 years

Software design will become much more human-centric and multidisciplinary. Engineers will guide agents using high-level design systems and ethical standards, treating code generation as a utility while spending their creative energy on user delight and seamless interactions.

## My hot take on AI

Prompt engineering is not the future of software engineering; thoughtful human design is.

# SG-35: Page structure

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Structure

A team website consists of these parts, in this order:

1. `<header>` with the group name, tagline and theme toggle
2. `<main>` containing:
   - `<section id="team">` – the team introduction and all member cards
   - `<section id="future-of-se">` – the team's shared view on AI and the future of software engineering,
     with the heading "The Future of Software Engineering"
3. `<footer>`, see the current footer document

The section ids are used for navigation links and MUST be exactly as given.
Additional sections (for example a "fun statistics" section) MAY be added between the two required sections.

--- Document SG-00: Scope ---
## Scope
The guide covers page structure, colors, theming, typography, responsive behaviour, content and tone.
It does not cover hosting, because team websites are delivered as a single local file.

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Color

The day mode uses a warm, paper-like look.

- Page background MUST be `#FFF8E7` (warm off-white).
- Main text color MUST be `#1D1D1F`.

# SG-50: Responsive breakpoints (version 2)

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Responsive

Team websites use exactly one layout breakpoint.

- The breakpoint MUST be written as `@media (max-width: 700px)`.
  The earlier, smaller breakpoint made cards too narrow on large phones.
- Below the breakpoint:
  - member cards are shown in one column
  - the header content is stacked vertically
  - side padding is reduced to 1rem
- The page MUST include `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">`.
- Test your page at 375 px and 1280 px width. There must be no horizontal scrolling.

# SG-19: Theme persistence (version 1)

Status: DEPRECATED – replaced by SG-21
Category: Theming

The theme choice of the user is remembered between visits.

- Store the choice in `localStorage` under the key `theme`.
- The stored value is either `light` or `dark`.
- Read the value when the page loads and apply it before the first paint.

--- Document SG-21: SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2) ---
# SG-21: Theme persistence (version 2)

Status: ACTIVE (version 2)
Category: Theming

The theme choice of the user is remembered between visits.

- The choice MUST be stored in `localStorage` under the key `upb-theme`.
  The old key was too generic and collided with other local files.
- The stored value is either `light` or `dark`.
- On page load, read the stored value. If there is none, follow the operating system preference.
- Apply the theme as early as possible to avoid a flash of the wrong theme.

# SG-18: Dark mode philosophy

Status: ACTIVE
Category: Theming

Users choose their theme, but we start with a sensible default.

- If the user has never chosen a theme, the page SHOULD follow the operating system preference (`prefers-color-scheme`).
- As soon as the user clicks the toggle, their choice wins and is remembered, see the theme persistence document.
- Switching the theme MUST NOT reload the page.

AI in engineering today

AI is unmatched for boilerplate and syntax lookups, but frequently hallucinates subtle logical flaws that make debugging twice as tedious. It speeds up typing without genuinely understanding architecture or context. Right now, it works best as an eager junior developer whose every commit needs thorough code review.

Looking 5–10 years ahead

The core job will shift from typing code to specifying requirements, edge cases, and architectural constraints. Autonomous agents may handle boilerplate; engineering value will center on verification, fault tolerance, and knowing what to build.

Hot take

“AI doesn’t make bad developers good; it just helps them generate catastrophic technical debt at record speed.”

AI in engineering today

AI assistants are fantastic productivity multipliers for well-understood domains and boilerplate, but break down in complex legacy enterprise codebases. They can be confidently wrong about synchronization primitives and concurrency. AI is a fast copilot—but you cannot let it navigate without senior oversight.

Looking 5–10 years ahead

Engineering will center on systems integration, prompt-driven formal verification, and distributed consensus rather than mundane feature programming. Junior roles may evolve into system orchestration, where failure modes and domain invariants matter more than low-level library APIs.

Hot take

“AI autocomplete hasn’t eliminated bugs; it has just made them compile much faster.”

Our shared perspective

The Future of Software Engineering

We see AI as a powerful change to how software gets made—not a substitute for engineering judgment. The work ahead is about giving automation the right constraints, checking what it produces, and keeping people at the center of the systems we build.

01

From typing to intent

As agents take on boilerplate and routine implementation, engineers can spend more time defining requirements, edge cases, system boundaries, and the outcomes a product should achieve.

02

Verification is the craft

Generated code still needs careful review. Reliability, concurrency, security, privacy, and fault tolerance demand people who understand the system and know how to test its assumptions.

03

Human context matters

Good software is more than code that compiles. Accessibility, thoughtful interfaces, domain understanding, and empathy help make technical systems useful and responsible for real people.

Use AI to move faster. Keep human judgment in charge of where you’re going.
